nameStory: The name Actinothoe comes from Greek words meaning 'ray' and 'swift,' referring to the radiating tentacles that can quickly retract when touched. The species name 'modesta' means 'modest' in Latin, perhaps reflecting this small anemone's unassuming appearance compared to its showier tide pool cousins.
description: The modest sea anemone is a small, delicate marine creature that looks like an underwater flower when its tentacles are extended. This soft-bodied animal typically measures only about half an inch across, making it one of the smaller anemones you'll encounter in New England waters. When disturbed, it can completely retract its tentacles and close up into a smooth, dome-shaped blob that's easily overlooked on rocky surfaces.

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Very small, typically under 0.5 inches across when fully extended, with a low, flattened profile rather than the tall column of larger anemones

idTips.label: Tentacle arrangement
idTips.description: Features numerous short, slender tentacles arranged in neat concentric circles around a small central mouth

idTips.label: Texture when closed
idTips.description: When retracted, feels firm and smooth like a small pebble, with a slightly sticky surface that may collect bits of sand or shell

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Ranges from pale cream to light brown or greenish, often with subtle darker markings on the column

idTips.label: Attachment style
idTips.description: Firmly attached to hard surfaces with a broad, flat base that's difficult to remove without damage

habitat: Found in rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal areas along New England's coast, particularly in protected coves and tide pools. Look for them attached to the undersides of rocks, in crevices, or on pier pilings where they're sheltered from strong waves. They prefer areas with good water circulation but not heavy surf action.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more active as water temperatures rise, with tentacles extended more frequently during calm weather and incoming tides.
seasonality.summer: Most easily observed during summer months when extended for longer periods. Low tide exploration offers the best viewing opportunities in tide pools.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may retract more quickly as temperatures drop and storm activity increases along the coast.
seasonality.winter: Often remains closed and inactive during coldest months, appearing as small bumps on rocks that are easily mistaken for barnacles or limpets.

funFact: Despite being only half an inch across, this tiny anemone can live for decades and has been observed to split itself in half to create an identical clone when conditions are favorable!
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for young specimens of larger anemone species, but the modest anemone maintains its small size throughout life. When closed, it can look like a small barnacle or limpet, but unlike those creatures, it will feel soft and slightly squishy rather than hard-shelled.
contextualKnowledge: Though called a 'modest' anemone, don't let the name fool you into thinking it's less interesting than larger species. Many beginning tide poolers overlook these small anemones entirely, missing out on observing one of the more common but understudied species in New England waters.
compareHints: **Note: Information about this rare species is limited - only 4 recorded observations in New England.** Compared to other small anemones in the Sagartiidae family, the modest anemone maintains a consistently flattened profile and smaller size. Unlike the similar-looking strawberry anemone, it lacks the distinctive warty texture and bright coloration, appearing more uniformly smooth and subdued in color.
